overview: These describe how a solution's solute concentration compares to the inside of a cell, predicting which way water will move.
genZNote: Hypotonic: cell drinks and swells. Hypertonic: cell gets squeezed dry. Isotonic: cell just chills, no net change.

aspects.label: Relative Solute Concentration
aspects.valueA: Hypotonic = lower solute outside than inside; Hypertonic = higher solute outside than inside.
aspects.valueB: Equal solute concentration inside and outside the cell.

aspects.label: Direction of Water Movement
aspects.valueA: Hypotonic: water moves INTO the cell. Hypertonic: water moves OUT of the cell.
aspects.valueB: No net movement of water in or out.

aspects.label: Effect on Cell
aspects.valueA: Hypotonic causes swelling (and lysis in animal cells); hypertonic causes shrinking (crenation in animal cells, plasmolysis in plant cells).
aspects.valueB: Cell maintains its normal size and shape.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Placing an RBC in distilled water (hypotonic) causes it to burst.
aspects.valueB: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is isotonic to human blood cells.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Plasmolysis (a plant cell shrinking away from its wall in a hypertonic solution) is a classic practical/viva demonstration.
overlay.memoryTrick: Hypotonic = cell gets fat (water in). Hypertonic = cell gets thin (water out).
overlay.commonMisconception: Isotonic doesn't mean 'no water movement at all' — water still moves both ways, but the net movement is zero.
